firstMessage.rawMarkdown:
AST-Augmented Dual-Agent Self-Correction: Improving Code Generation and Repair with Lightweight Gemma 4 Models via Execution-Feedback Loops

Author: Saiyyad Ahmed  
Track: Gemma 4 Developer Agent – Paper Track



Abstract
Large frontier models dominate software-engineering agents, yet running them locally on consumer hardware remains impractical. We present **A2-DASC (AST-Augmented Dual-Agent Self-Correction)**, a lightweight agentic framework that substantially improves a small Gemma 4 model on code generation and repair through an iterative execution-feedback loop, without any weight updates. A Generator proposes candidate solutions. A Critic, drawn from the same checkpoint, receives the runtime traceback, the failing test case, and a compact AST-based structural summary, then returns a short repair instruction. On a curated suite of 120 tasks covering single-function generation, semantic repair, and multi-module problems, A2-DASC raises the pass@1 of **Gemma 4 12B Unified** from **41.7% (zero-shot) to 78.3%** after at most three iterations (mean of 5 independent runs, 95% CI [69.2%–85.8%]). Ablations isolate the critical contributions of AST context and the distinct Critic role. We further report inference cost (tokens and wall-clock time), showing that structured feedback is a more efficient scaling path on consumer GPUs than simply using a larger model. All code, prompts, and evaluation harness are publicly released for full reproducibility.

1. Introduction
Autonomous coding agents have advanced rapidly, but the strongest systems still depend on massive closed models that cannot run efficiently on laptops or a single consumer GPU. This creates a clear accessibility barrier.

Rather than forcing a small model to solve complex problems in one forward pass, we treat code generation as an iterative, environment-grounded process: generate, execute in a sandbox, observe the failure, inspect structural differences, and refine. A2-DASC implements this loop for lightweight models.

Contributions:
* A dual-role architecture (Generator + AST-Augmented Critic) that uses a single small-model checkpoint, differing only in prompt and input schema.
* A compact, leakage-free AST structural summary that is injected into the Critic together with the traceback and failing test.
* A controlled empirical study with ablations, confidence intervals, and a detailed cost analysis of the refinement loop.
* A fully local, sandboxed, reproducible implementation designed for consumer hardware, with all artifacts publicly released.

 2. Related Work
Self-correction via execution feedback has been studied in Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023), Self-Debug (Chen et al., 2023), and related environment loops. Most prior systems either assume large frontier models or supply only free-form text feedback. Repository-level agents such as SWE-agent (Yang et al., 2024) rely on heavy toolchains and long contexts that are poorly suited to small local models. Recent in-stream repair approaches (e.g., SecReason, 2026) focus on decoding-time fixes rather than multi-turn structural refinement.

A2-DASC differs in three respects: (1) the Critic receives structured AST information in addition to the traceback, (2) the entire system is designed to run on a single consumer GPU, and (3) we explicitly measure the gain of structured feedback over unstructured text feedback on a lightweight model.

 3. Method
3.1 Overall Loop
1. Generation: he Generator receives the natural-language specification and produces a candidate Python solution.
2. Sandbox Execution: The candidate is executed in an isolated Docker sandbox (strict CPU/RAM limits, no network, 5-second timeout) against the unit tests.
3. Feedback Capture: On failure we record the raw traceback, the exact failing assertion or exception, and the failing input with expected versus actual output.
4. Critique: The Critic receives the problem statement, previous code, traceback, AST summary, and failing-test details, then outputs a concise repair instruction.
5. Refinement: The Generator conditions on the instruction and produces a new candidate. The loop stops when all tests pass or after a maximum of three iterations.

No-leakage rule: The AST summary is computed solely between the current attempt and the immediately preceding attempt. We never compare against a reference solution.

3.2 AST-Augmented Critic
Using Python’s native `ast` module we extract a compact structural view:
* Function and class signatures.
* Control-flow skeleton (loops, conditionals, returns).
* Variables and lines that appear in the traceback.
* Explicit list of AST nodes that changed relative to the previous attempt.

Both Generator and Critic are instantiated from the same Gemma 4 12B Unified checkpoint. Only the system prompt and input schema differ. No weights are updated.

 4. Experimental Setup
4.1 Task Suite
We evaluate on 120 problems divided into three balanced groups:
Single-function generation (40 tasks): selected from HumanEval and LiveCodeBench (2026 subset)
Semantic repair (40 tasks): operator errors, off-by-one bugs, and missing edge cases
Multi-module tasks (40 tasks):coordination across 2–4 files

Contamination checks confirmed no overlap with documented training data of the Gemma 4 family.

4.2 Baselines
* Zero-shot Gemma 4 12B Unified
* Zero-shot Gemma 4 31B Dense
* Unstructured feedback (traceback only)
* Single-model self-refine (traceback + AST, no separate Critic)
* Frontier model, single-shot (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, 20241022)

4.3 Implementation Details
All runs used a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24 GB) with 4-bit quantization. Decoding was fixed at temperature 0.2, top-p 0.95. Results are means of 5 independent runs with fixed seeds. The complete code, prompts, and evaluation harness are publicly released at https://github.com to ensure full reproducibility.

 5. Results
 5 5.1 Main Results

| Method | pass@1 (0 iter) | pass@1 (≤3 iter) | 95% CI | Avg. iters | Avg. tokens | Avg. time (s) |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Gemma 4 12B (Zero-shot) | 41.7% | 41.7% | [32.8–51.1] | – | 1.2k | 4.1 |
| Gemma 4 12B + Unstructured | 41.7% | 64.2% | [54.9–72.6] | 2.1 | 4.8k | 14.2 |
| **Gemma 4 12B + A2-DASC (Ours)** | **41.7%** | **78.3%** | **[69.2–85.8]** | **1.7** | **3.9k** | **11.5** |
| Gemma 4 31B (Zero-shot) | 68.3% | 68.3% | [59.1–76.3] | – | 1.5k | 8.9 |
| Frontier Model (Single-shot) | 84.2% | 84.2% | [76.2–90.1] | – | 2.2k | 5.4 |

A2-DASC recovers 36.6 absolute points over zero-shot 12B and surpasses zero-shot 31B while using substantially less VRAM footprint on consumer devices.

 5.2 Results by Task Group

| Group | Zero-shot | Unstructured | A2-DASC (Ours) |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Generation | 52.5% | 72.5% | 85.0% |
| Semantic Repair | 45.0% | 67.5% | 82.5%|
| Multi-module | 27.5% | 52.5% | 67.5%|

 5.3 Ablations

| Variant | Traceback | AST Summary | Separate Critic | pass@1 (≤3) |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Full A2-DASC** | yes | yes| yes | 78.3%|
| No AST | yes | no | yes | 67.5% |
| No separate Critic | yes | yes | no | 61.7% |
| Traceback only | yes | no | no | 64.2% |
| Failing test only | no | no | no | 48.3% |

 5.4 Cost Analysis
A2-DASC averages 3.9k tokens and 11.5 seconds per completed task on the 12B model. Moving to the 31B zero-shot baseline increases both memory footprint and per-token latency. Structured feedback therefore provides a more efficient path to higher accuracy on consumer hardware than raw parameter scaling.

6. Discussion & Conclusion
The results indicate that high-quality structured feedback can successfully substitute for a substantial increase in model size on code generation and repair tasks. By combining runtime tracebacks with a compact AST structural summary inside a specialized Critic role, the method recovers 36.6 absolute points over zero-shot performance and surpasses a larger 31B zero-shot baseline. All artifacts are publicly released via GitHub to support further research on local-first developer agents.
